did_you_know.text: The name Yam Suph is sometimes translated as “Sea of Reeds,” because the Hebrew word *suph* can refer to reeds. Scholars do not all agree on the exact location of the sea in the story.
The rebellion of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram is described in Numbers 16. The phrase “all their possessions” includes their property and everything connected with their households.
“A land flowing with milk and honey” describes a land rich in pasture and agricultural produce. In the Bible, “honey” can also mean fruit syrup, such as date syrup, not only bee honey.
The comparison with Egypt reflects farming that depended on the Nile and irrigation canals. “You water it with your foot” probably describes laborious, hands-on irrigation work.
In ancient Israel, farming depended largely on winter rains, unlike Egypt, which depended on the Nile. The timing of rain was therefore especially important for planting and harvests.
The *yoreh* is the first rain of the season, while the *malkosh* is the late rain that helps the grain mature. Together, the words describe the agricultural rain cycle in the land.
The phrases “as a sign on your hand” and “between your eyes” became the basis for the Jewish practice of wearing tefillin. Tefillin contain passages from the Torah, including the Shema sections.
This verse presents education as more than a school lesson: people learn at home, on the road, before sleep, and in the morning. Learning is portrayed as part of everyday life.
This verse is the source of the practice of affixing a mezuzah to a doorway. Inside it is a scroll containing the Shema passages, including verses from Deuteronomy 11.

The Euphrates lies to the east, in the region of modern Iraq and Syria, while “the western sea” is usually identified as the Mediterranean. The boundary here is a broad description of the Promised Land, not a modern political map.

Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal are near Shechem, in the hills of Samaria. Gerizim lies south of the valley and Ebal north of it, making the site suitable for a ceremony proclaiming blessing and curse together.
